Downstream auditing (and any logic that keys off `matchedStep`) will attribute the match to the wrong provider at the highest confidence tier. Give `rekordboxId` its own step (or drop the `??` fallback) so `matchedStep` reflects the real source.

The path-based branch emits `step: "title-path"`, the same id used by the title branch below. When the path lookup fails and the title path then matches, `steps` contains two consecutive `"title-path"` outcomes with different confidences (0 / 0.5), and `matchedStep` cannot tell a caller which mechanism actually resolved the track. Use a distinct step id (e.g. `"path-library"`) for the path branch. Also, the `note: "path not in library"` is inaccurate when `libraryByPath` returned a row that simply lacks a `rekordboxId` — the row was found, so the message misleads debugging.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/identity..content: All three external lookup hooks (`libraryById`, `libraryByPath`, `titleIndex`) are invoked with optional chaining but no error handling. A single throw from any hook (DB/IPC failure) propagates out of `resolveLiveTrack`, aborting the entire DS-22 chain and skipping every lower-priority step and the title fallback — the exact failover behaviour the chain exists to provide. Wrap each hook call in try/catch (recording a failed step outcome) so the chain continues to the next step.

The identity-parts assembly (`...row`, `rekordboxId` fallback, `fileHash`/`pcmFingerprint` merge) and the `resolveTrackId` call are duplicated across the id-step loop, the path branch, and the title branch, and they diverge: the path branch passes `row` verbatim, dropping the input `fileHash`/`pcmFingerprint` that the id steps include, so a moved/renamed file cannot attach via hash on the path step. Extract a single helper (e.g. `resolveWithParts(parts, hash, fingerprint)`) so every step applies the same merge rules.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/prolink-prov.content: On bind failure the socket is never closed: the `catch` re-throws without calling `socket.close()`, leaving the UDP socket (and its `reuseAddr` bound port) leaked, while `this.socket` still references it. Additionally two `error` listeners are registered for the same event (the persistent `socket.on("error", ...)` and `socket.once("error", onError)`), so a bind error fires both handlers and sets two different failed statuses. Close the socket (and null out `this.socket`) before re-throwing, and keep only one error path.

The socket is created without `setBroadcast(true)`, but `tick()` later sends to the broadcast address `255.255.255.255`. Without enabling broadcast, most platforms reject the datagram with EACCES/ENETUNREACH, so virtual-CDJ keepalives never reach the network. Enable broadcast on the socket.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/providers.ts.content: Generation bump is keyed on the fabricated track id, and `toTrack` collapses every id-less track to the shared literal `"unknown"`. Because the comparison uses `(incoming?.id ?? null)`, loading two *distinct* tracks that both lack an `id` yields `"unknown" !== "unknown"` → false, so `generation` is never incremented. Every downstream consumer that keys on `generation` (fusion, loop-roll, hot-cue/phrase reset) then keeps serving the previous track's fields, violating the header contract ("every provider increments `generation` on track load, unload and replacement"). Fix by deriving identity from a stable composite (id ∪ canonicalPath ∪ title/artist) and never mapping two different tracks onto the same `"unknown"` sentinel.

`this.beats` is never cleared when `generation` increments, and when a hint omits `beat` (i.e. `hint.beat === undefined`) the mapper silently reuses the cached beat from the *previous* generation. After a track load/unload the emitted state therefore carries the old track's `beat` value, directly breaking the stated invariant "never emits a field belonging to the previous generation after the increment". Clear the per-deck caches (`beats`, and any other generation-scoped state) inside the generation-bump branch so a new generation starts clean.

const beat = hint.beat === undefined ? (this.beats.get(deckId) ?? null) : hint.beat;
    if (beat !== null) this.beats.set(deckId, beat);

packages/rekordbox-live/src/providers.ts.content: `started` is set to `true` *before* `await this.onStart()`, with no error handling. Real providers do reject here (e.g. `Os2lProvider.onStart` re-throws bind failures and `SeratoRemoteProvider.onStart` re-throws client start failures), so: (1) `this.started` remains `true` after a failed start and all subsequent `start()` retries are silently swallowed; (2) a later `stop()` will set `started = false` and call `onStop()` on a provider whose `onStart()` never completed; (3) concurrent `start()` callers return before initialization finishes. Reset `started` on failure (and surface the error) so the lifecycle stays consistent. `stop()` has the mirror problem: `started` is cleared before `onStop()` runs, so a rejecting `onStop()` is not retryable and can leak resources.

Two problems in `emit`. (1) The monotonic-timestamp fix reassigns a *copy* to the local `state`, so listeners receive the corrected `receivedAtNs` while the object the caller stores/returns (e.g. `ScriptedProvider.update`'s `merged`, `this.decks.set(...)`) keeps the stale timestamp. `getDecks()` consumers and event listeners therefore observe different `receivedAtNs` values, and the documented "monotonic timestamps" guarantee only holds for one of them. Mutate the received object instead (or return the adjusted state and have callers use it). (2) `this.queueDepth = Math.min(1, this.queueDepth + 1)` pins `queueDepth` to 1 forever — it is never decremented — so `getStats().queueDepth` is a meaningless constant and can never report a drain.

`quality` (and `fieldSources`) are rebuilt from scratch on every update, so any label not present in the current `hint.quality` is discarded even for deck fields that are unchanged. A provider that reports quality incrementally (e.g. only the fields touched by a given message) will silently lose the labels established by earlier updates, and downstream fusion/quality consumers will see `undefined` for still-valid fields. Merge into the previously stored labels rather than replacing. Also note `fieldSources` only ever labels `track`, `playing`, `playheadSeconds`, `effectiveBpm` (+ optional faders) — fields like `beat`, `beatInBar`, `pitchPercent`, `sync`, `loopRoll`, `lastHotCue`, `phrase`, `loop` and `master` are set on the state but get no source label.

packages/storage/src/session.ts.content: Byte budget mismatch: `maxBytes` is derived from `maxMb` as true bytes, but record sizes are measured with `JSON.stringify(entry).length`, which counts UTF-16 code units, not encoded bytes (and also mishandles surrogate pairs). For non-ASCII payloads the buffer silently exceeds the configured budget and eviction thresholds are wrong. Compute the size with `Buffer.byteLength(JSON.stringify(entry), "utf8")` (and use the same measure when subtracting evicted entries).

`stableHash` relies on `JSON.stringify`, whose output depends on object key insertion order. Two semantically identical inputs/config snapshots built with different key order produce different hashes, so `frameHashFor` is not a stable determinism check and replay can report false mismatches (or should-be mismatches can be masked). Serialize with a canonical form (recursively sorted keys) before hashing.

`split("\n")` yields empty trailing/middle segments for NDJSON with a trailing newline or blank lines, and `JSON.parse("")` then throws `invalid JSON` for a perfectly valid file (exportNdjson itself produces no trailing newline, so a round-tripped file with an added newline breaks). Filter out empty lines before parsing. Also `row.kind` is cast to `SessionKind` without validating it against the allowed union, so unknown kinds are silently accepted.

Replay passes `inputs.get(tick)` straight into `render`; when a frame-hash tick has no matching `tick-input` record (or when duplicate tick-inputs collide via last-write-wins), the renderer is invoked with `undefined`/wrong inputs and the mismatch is silently recorded without surfacing the real cause. Distinguish "missing input" from an explicit `undefined` input and report it (e.g. add to `mismatchedTicks` or throw) instead of rendering with unknown inputs.

analysis/tests/test_config_bridge.py.content: The guard only matches decimal float literals (`\d+\.\d+`), so hardcoded *integer* tuning constants are never flagged (e.g. `minVotes = 3`, `minAnchors = 32`, `windows = (8, 16, 32)`). Given the detection must see a numeric literal on the line, integer thresholds slip through silently, giving a false sense of enforcement. Match integers too, e.g. `\d+(?:\.\d+)?`.

The skip condition `"config" in low` is a broad substring match: ANY line whose text merely contains the letters “config” is exempted — including comments such as `min_votes = 3  # not from config` or a stray mention of “configuration”. A hardcoded tuning value on such a line is hidden from the check, defeating the test’s purpose. Restrict the exemption to actual config reads (e.g. `cfg.get(`/`cfg[`), not an arbitrary substring.

The skip list and the detection list use different casing for the same concepts (`min_anchors`/`tolerance_ms` vs `minAnchors`/`tolerance`), and the real sources use snake_case (`min_votes`, `min_strength`, `min_anchors`, `tolerance_ms`). Therefore a genuinely hardcoded assignment like `min_anchors = 32` or `tolerance_ms = 0.05` is explicitly skipped, while the camelCase detection keywords only ever occur inside `cfg.get("analysis...minAnchors")` strings (already skipped). Net effect: the test can never flag a real offender. Use consistent, snake_case-aware keywords in both lists.

`test_defaults_match_schema` only compares key sets, so a default whose *value* disagrees with the schema (wrong magnitude, wrong type, drifted threshold) still passes — the test name promises a match it never verifies. Consider also asserting the value in `defaults[k]` equals `schema["properties"][k].get("default")` where a default is declared, which is the actual invariant being claimed.

If an IPC round-trip takes longer than the interval, polls overlap and a late response can land after a newer one, writing a stale beat into `beatRef` (and `set`), making the cursor jump backwards. This mutates state shared with the mount-fetch path and can silently clobber a plan the show host computed (e.g. a different venue/planner version), while burning CPU 4x/sec. Compile only when the style actually changes and keep the loaded plan immutable (or cache by trackId+styleId).
